claims.claim: Evidence-based practice means making care decisions by combining the best available research evidence, clinical expertise, and patient values and preferences — the three-part 'EBP triad' of scientific evidence, clinical experience, and patient values.
The EBP movement has decreased the gap between what nurses and other healthcare professionals do in practice and what they should do based on the best evidence.

Evidence-based practice bundles — small sets of evidence-based interventions used together — have been shown to improve patient outcomes, including reducing hospital-acquired complications such as ventilator-associated pneumonia and central line-associated bloodstream infections.

Research evidence comes in layers: high-quality systematic reviews are the preferred evidence, and guidelines and recommendations (such as those published by CDC) help decision makers choose courses of action.

EBP is a structured process: when a nurse meets a clinical question, the nurse uses the steps of EBP to seek relevant research and find an answer that aligns with the nurse's experience and the patient's preferences and values.

Evidence informs but does not dictate: even when the best evidence supports an intervention and it fits clinical expertise and patient preferences, it may still be impossible to provide because of agency policies, procedural concerns, or resource limitations, so decisions reflect the evidence plus the situational reality of the setting.

Evidence-based practice relies on scientific evidence rather than anecdotal evidence, and not all health information found in the media or online is trustworthy, so evaluating information is part of using evidence well.
The modern evidence-based medicine movement is associated with the 1996 BMJ editorial 'Evidence based medicine: what it is and what it isn't' by David Sackett and colleagues.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Different sources define evidence-based practice with slightly different wording, and some formulations add a fourth element — the practice setting and its resources.
positions: OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing teaches the EBP triad of scientific evidence, clinical experience, and patient values, while separately noting that decisions are also shaped by the setting, policies, and resources.
The 1996 Sackett BMJ editorial emphasizes pairing the clinician's expertise with the best available external evidence from systematic research.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the three-part model (best research evidence, clinical expertise, patient values and preferences) attributed to OpenStax Fundamentals of Nursing, and covers the setting element through the 'evidence informs, it does not dictate' honest note rather than merging it into the triad.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The number and names of the EBP process steps vary across models.
positions: OpenStax describes 'the steps of EBP' without presenting one canonical numbered list.
Popular teaching models present five steps with slightly different verbs (ask, search/acquire, appraise, apply/integrate, evaluate/assess).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches a simple five-step version — ask, find, appraise, apply, evaluate — as an accessible simplification consistent with the structured-process claim, and notes that models vary in wording.

sourceRecords.title: CDC - Evidence-Based Practices - Health System Resource (STLT Gateway)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
sourceRecords.notes: Reused from the phase-4 source registry (identical id and URL). CDC's gateway page on evidence-based practices compiles resources for evidence-based programs and policies (ACIP recommendations, CDC Guidelines and Recommendations, The Community Guide, USPSTF) and describes CDC guidelines and recommendations as helping decision makers choose courses of action. Supports the guidelines-and-recommendations evidence layer and the evidence-informs-decisions framing. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Fundamentals of Nursing, Section 15.1: Evidence-Based Research
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: the steps of EBP — when a nurse has a question, the nurse can use the steps of EBP to seek relevant research and find an answer that aligns with the nurse's experience and the patient's preferences and values; high-quality systematic reviews published within the last five years as the preferred evidence; the ANA research-standard language of combining evidence-based information with personal experience and patient preferences; the history of nursing research and EBP. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Fundamentals of Nursing, Section 15.2: Evidence-Based Clinical Decisions
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: EBP as using evidence when making decisions about caring for individual patients; the EBP triad of scientific evidence, clinical experience, and patient values; the EBP movement decreasing the gap between what nurses and other healthcare professionals do in practice and what they should do based on the best evidence; evidence-based practice bundles as small sets of evidence-based interventions used together to improve patient outcomes (e.g., ventilator-associated pneumonia and central line-associated bloodstream infections); the point that even gold-standard care supported by evidence, clinical expertise, and patient preferences may be impossible because of agency policies, procedural concerns, or resource limitations, so decisions reflect the triad plus the situational reality of the setting; patient preferences as a key tenet of patient-centered care and shared decision-making. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Evaluating Health Information
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: health information from newspapers, magazines, books, TV, the Internet, and social media is not all up to date and trustworthy, so it is important to evaluate it; two key steps — ask questions before trusting what you read or hear, and discuss the information with your health care provider. Used for the honest note that not all health information is reliable and that evaluating information is part of using evidence well. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Nutrition: 1.5 Evidence-Based Practice and Nutrition (Nutrition for Nurses, 2e)
sourceRecords.notes: Reused from the phase-4 source registry (identical id and URL). Read via Wayback capture (web.archive.org/web/20240412142715). Supports: evidence-based practice uses scientific evidence rather than anecdotal evidence; only some nutrition information available online is vetted for appropriateness and validity. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Evidence based medicine: what it is and what it isn't (BMJ 1996;312:71-72)
sourceRecords.provider: BMJ; bibliographic record verified via PubMed (NCBI)
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record verified 2026-08-22 via NCBI E-utilities (PubMed PMID 8555924; PMCID PMC2349778; BMJ 1996 Jan 13;312(7023):71-2; authors Sackett DL, Rosenberg WM, Gray JA, Haynes RB, Richardson WS). Full text was not retrievable in this session (bmj.com returns 403 and PMC serves a script-rendered viewer), so this record is used ONLY for the historical attribution that the modern evidence-based medicine movement is associated with this 1996 BMJ editorial and its title. No claims about the editorial's wording are made from this source.
